name: PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
venue: NAACL 2024 (Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the ACL: Human Language Technologies, Volume 1: Long Papers, pages 6537-6555; ACL Anthology 2024.naacl-long.364; DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.naacl-long.364). Also arXiv:2406.12430.
authors_affiliation: Myeonghwa Lee* (myeon9h), Seonho An* (asho1), Min-Soo Kim+ (corresponding author, minsoo.k). *Equal contribution; +corresponding. All affiliated with the School of Computing, KAIST (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology).
code_url: https://github.com/myeon9h/PlanRAG (MIT license; ~154 stars; contributors Myeonghwa Lee and Seonho An; Python; includes DQA benchmark data, game simulators, and src/main.py with --technique {PlanRAG,IterRAG,SingleRAG}).
maintained_repo_url: N/A (single research repo for this paper; last substantive commits 2024; not a continuously-updated leaderboard/paper list).
task_domain: decision-making (LLM-as-decision-maker) over structured data; framed as Decision QA, a QA-style task that requires complex data analysis over a large database to answer the best decision. Spans both relational (RDB) and labeled-property-graph (GDB) databases.
problem_setting: Offline, single-agent, non-interactive, zero-shot, single-run. The authors define Decision QA: given a decision-making question Q (containing a textual goal), business rules R (textual descriptions of formulas referenced to reason the best decision), and a structured database D following schema S, the LM must output the best decision d_best. D is assumed too large to fit in the LM context at once, so the LM must issue data-analysis queries (SQL for RDB via MySQL, Cypher/CQL for GDB via Neo4j) to retrieve scattered pieces of data, possibly iteratively. No human-annotated reasoning supervision is given; the base LM (GPT-4, zero temperature) is frozen and used purely via prompting (ReAct-style). Zero-shot is deliberately chosen because (1) real-world business decision strategies are usually unknown in advance and (2) few-shot examples cause overfitting to both the solving strategy and the database content of the shots. The single-LM implementation performs both planning and retrieval/answer reasoning.
what_is_retrieved: Structured data records from a database D: rows/tuples from RDB tables (e.g., TradingNode, Country, TradingFlow, NodeCountry for Locating; Goods, Buildings, Demand, Supply for Building) or vertices/edges from a labeled property graph, returned by executing LM-generated SQL/Cypher data-analysis queries. Not text documents; the retrieval target is the agent-queried structured database content needed for the analysis (e.g., flows, trading powers, supply/demand values).
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external structured store. Each Decision QA instance is grounded on a fixed, given database D (an RDB in MySQL or an LPG/graph DB in Neo4j) that is queried via SQL/Cypher. There is no agent-written growing/episodic memory; the database is read-only and not augmented with stored experiences during deployment.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Completeness-of-needed-data oriented rather than fixed top-k ranking. Success depends on the LM retrieving/calculating ALL critical intermediate values required by the business rules (e.g., IV and TP_total for Locating; CO and PD for Building); the paper explicitly measures 'rate of missed data analysis' (1.3% / 21.8% for PlanRAG vs 3.3% / 33.2% for IterRAG) as the completeness of the analysis. There is no relevance-ranked top-k document set; queries return exactly the structured records they request (SQL/Cypher result sets).
retrieval_unit: Database query result set: tuples/rows from RDB tables or vertices/edges (and their properties) from a labeled property graph, obtained by executing an LM-generated SQL or Cypher data-analysis query. Effectively (structured-record) granularity, not token/snippet/document.
index_source: Static, given structured database per question (no offline-induced or online-induced retrievable memory store). The DQA benchmark provides D in two forms (RDB and GDB) for each question; D is loaded into MySQL / Neo4j and queried live via SQL/Cypher at test time. The store is frozen (read-only) and does not grow.
index_structure_topology: Database-native organization: a relational schema (tables with keys/foreign keys, 4 tables per scenario) for the RDB version, and a labeled property graph (vertices + edges with properties) for the GDB version. So the retrievable store is a structured DB schema / property graph, not a flat vector index. Access is via DBMS query execution rather than embedding similarity.
retriever_type: LLM-as-retriever via generated database queries: the same GPT-4-based LM writes SQL (for RDB) or Cypher/CQL (for GDB) data-analysis queries that are executed against the DBMS (MySQL / Neo4j) through RAG interfaces (LangChain / LlamaIndex). No BM25/dense embedding retriever; retrieval is query generation + DBMS execution.
retriever_learning_signal: none (off-the-shelf / training-free). The retriever is the frozen GPT-4 LM prompted (zero-shot, zero temperature) to emit SQL/Cypher queries; nothing is trained or fine-tuned. The paper explicitly leaves fine-tuning a Cypher-query generator as future work (Limitations). Query 'selection' is driven by the generated plan, not by a learned similarity/RL signal.
query_construction: Plan-conditioned generation of executable data-analysis queries. In the planning step the LM examines <Q, S, R> (question, DB schema, business rules) and produces an initial natural-language plan describing the series of analyses needed; in the retrieving step the LM consumes <Q, S, R, plan> and generates concrete SQL/Cypher queries to fetch the scattered data. Re-planning regenerates the plan conditioned on intermediate query results. (Baseline IterRAG/SingleRAG generate queries directly from <Q, S, R> without an explicit plan, following ReAct Thought-Action-Observation.)
query_granularity: Two-level: a task-level plan is formed at t=0 over the whole question (and re-formed during re-planning), and step-level data-analysis queries are then issued iteratively within the retrieving step according to the plan.
when_to_retrieve: Iterative (multi-turn). PlanRAG repeats planning + retrieving steps, with the LM deciding after each retrieval whether to (a) continue with a further retrieval, (b) re-plan, or (c) answer. SingleRAG retrieves once; IterRAG retrieves multiple times. PlanRAG adds the plan/re-plan control on top of the iterative loop.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Agent-initiated / LM self-assessment. After each retrieval step the LM assesses (via the 'Re-plan' instruction in the Plan-Thought-Action-Observation-Re-plan prompt) whether the current plan and retrieved query results are sufficient: if not, it triggers either a further retrieval or a re-plan; if sufficient, it answers. There is no fixed schedule, token-confidence, attention, or learned classifier trigger - it is prompt-driven self-assessment by the single LM.
reranking: None. Retrieved data are exact DBMS query results (SQL/Cypher), not a ranked candidate list; there is no cross-encoder/RRF/instruction-tuned reranking stage.
retrieved_context_refinement: None beyond the plan/re-plan control loop. Query results (Observations) are fed back into the ReAct-style reasoning; there is no decompose-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of retrieved records. The novelty is in better-targeted query generation (via planning), not in post-retrieval refinement.
how_retrieved_used: Prompt augmentation within a ReAct loop: query results are inserted as 'Observation' steps into the LM's reasoning context and used to (i) reason whether to re-plan / retrieve further and (ii) compute the business-rule-derived values needed for the final decision. The LM ultimately generates d_best (the answering step) grounded on the accumulated retrieved data and the plan.
planning_integration: Plan-then-retrieve (iterative). PlanRAG interleaves two reasoning types in a single LM: (1) planning - generate an initial analysis plan from <Q, S, R> before any retrieval; (2) retrieving & answering - generate/execute SQL/Cypher queries guided by the plan and reason over results; (3) re-planning - if the current plan is insufficient (assessed from query results), generate a new plan and loop back. Implemented by adding 'Plan' and 'Re-plan' instructions to a ReAct (Thought-Action-Observation) backbone, giving a Plan-Thought-Action-Observation-Re-plan structure.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-tool-call within a rollout (per query/retrieval step): each iteration is a Thought-Action(query)-Observation cycle, with a global Plan step preceding the loop and Re-plan steps inserted between retrievals when needed. Retrieval is woven in at the granularity of individual database queries (actions) inside the reasoning trajectory.
retrieved_item_representation: Raw structured query results (SQL result rows / Cypher graph results, i.e., the values and records returned by the DBMS) surfaced as ReAct 'Observation' text in the prompt. No distillation into strategies/guidelines/programs; the injected items are the literal retrieved data values.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Raw retrieved data records/values (low abstraction). The retrieved unit is concrete database content (rows, edges, computed/aggregated values), not a distilled strategy, workflow, skill, or hint. The plan itself is an abstraction produced by the LM, but what is RETRIEVED remains raw structured data.
noise_robustness_mechanism: No dedicated noise/distractor mechanism. Because retrieval is exact DBMS query execution rather than approximate similarity search, irrelevant-document noise is largely avoided by construction. The implicit robustness lever is the planning/re-planning loop, which reduces 'missed data analysis' (MIS) and improper-candidate (CAN) errors relative to IterRAG (per the failure-case analysis); there is no retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, or distractor-aware SFT.
memory_type: none (no persistent episodic/skill/workflow/procedural memory). The only across-iteration state is the current plan and accumulated Observations within a single question's ReAct trajectory, which is not stored or reused across questions.
write_back: false. No experiences, cases, plans, or skills are written into any persistent store for later retrieval; each Decision QA instance is solved independently.
online_growth: false. The queried database is fixed (read-only) per question and is not augmented during deployment; no retrievable store grows at test time.
write_back_trigger: never (no memory write-back exists). The intermediate plan is regenerated (re-planning) within the same trajectory but is not persisted to any cross-question memory.
failure_experience_usage: Not stored/reused as retrievable experience. Failures are only analyzed offline by the authors (five error categories: CAN improper candidates, MIS missed data analysis, DEEP misuse of retrieved data/equations, QUR query-generation error, OTH other) to explain results; within a run, an insufficient/failed plan triggers re-planning, but no failure memory is saved for future questions.
memory_evolution_update: N/A (no persistent stored entries). Within a single trajectory the plan can be replaced/refined via re-planning (refine-overwrite of the current plan), but there is no cross-episode memory mutation.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No. Retrieval (query generation and the decide-to-retrieve/re-plan/answer control) is driven by zero-shot prompting of a frozen GPT-4, not by any learned/RL/value-based policy or trained top-k selector.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: N/A (single-agent, single-LM design; the authors explicitly note multi-LM frameworks are out of scope and left as future work). No cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.
benchmarks: DQA (Decision QA benchmark), introduced by this paper, with two scenarios: Locating (from the game Europa Universalis IV) and Building (from the game Victoria 3). 301 (Q, D) pairs total (200 Locating, 101 Building); each question provided in both RDB and GDB versions, giving 602 databases. Compared against Tabular QA / Table NLI benchmarks (HybridQA, TAT-QA, FinQA, WikiTableQA, TabFact, ToTTo-TNLI) only to contrast database size (avg rows per table), not as evaluation tasks.
benchmark_family: decision-making over structured databases (a new benchmark family proposed here, DQA). Not in the standard QA/web/embodied/tool/code/memory/decision-RL families; closest neighbor is structured-data reasoning (Tabular QA / Table NLI), but DQA adds business rules R and large database querying (SQL/Cypher) for best-decision selection.
baselines: SingleRAG-LM (single-turn RAG); IterRAG-LM (iterative RAG, treated as the state-of-the-art iterative RAG technique, implemented with a ReAct Thought-Action-Observation prompt structure following Yao et al. 2023); and PlanRAG-LM w/o RP (PlanRAG without re-planning, internal ablation). All built on GPT-4 (zero temperature, zero-shot, LangChain). Additional model-variation baselines in the appendix: IterRAG-LM vs PlanRAG-LM implemented with GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, Llama-2 (70B), Llama-2 (13B), and Phi-2.
key_metrics: Accuracy (%) - an answer is correct only if it is semantically identical to the ground-truth best decision; reported as the average of RDB and GDB accuracies per scenario. Supporting/process metrics: rate of missed data analysis (%), SR (single-retrieval) vs MR (multiple-retrieval) accuracy breakdown, failure-case category distribution (CAN/MIS/DEEP/QUR/OTH), and number of re-plannings vs accuracy.
headline_result: PlanRAG-LM (GPT-4) achieves 64.3% accuracy on Locating and 45.0% on Building, outperforming the SOTA iterative RAG (IterRAG-LM: 48.5% / 37.6%) by 15.8 percentage points on Locating and 7.4 percentage points on Building (the paper states '15.8%' and '7.4%' improvements). SingleRAG-LM scores 30.5% / 2.5%.
ablations: (1) Re-planning ablation (Table 4): removing re-planning (PlanRAG-LM w/o RP) drops accuracy to 53.5% Locating / 44.1% Building, i.e., -10.8% Locating and -0.9% Building vs full PlanRAG, showing re-planning is important (especially for Locating). (2) RDB vs GDB (Table 5): PlanRAG best in both; PlanRAG more effective for GDB than RDB on Building (40.6% RDB vs 49.5% GDB) due to longer traversals. (3) SR vs MR difficulty split (Figure 5; 84 SR pairs, 518 MR pairs): PlanRAG's gain over IterRAG is larger on SR questions (questions IterRAG underestimated as single-retrieval). (4) Rate of missed data analysis (Table 6): PlanRAG 1.3%/21.8% vs IterRAG 3.3%/33.2%. (5) Failure-case analysis (Figure 6): PlanRAG sharply reduces CAN and MIS errors, with slightly more DEEP errors as a side effect. (6) Prompt-structure ablation (Table 10, 10% subset): Plan-Thought-Action-Observation-Re-plan (57.5/50) beats IterRAG Thought-Action-Observation (37.5/30) and the variants Plan-Action-Observation-Re-plan (40/40) and Thought-Plan-Action-Observation-Re-plan (27.5/30), showing the planning step's placement matters and 'Thought' must precede the action. (7) Re-planning frequency vs accuracy (Table 7): accuracy declines as the number of re-plannings rises; Building re-plans far more often (38% of questions) than Locating (6%). (8) Model ablation (Table 11): with GPT-3.5, Llama-2 70B/13B, Phi-2, both methods collapse - Llama-2/Phi-2 solve 0; under GPT-3.5 IterRAG slightly beats PlanRAG because the PlanRAG prompt is too complex; GPT-4 is required.
evaluation_decoupling: Partially. The primary metric is the end-to-end decision accuracy, but the paper also reports an intrinsic process metric - the 'rate of missed data analysis' (whether the critical values were ever queried/computed) - decoupled from final accuracy (e.g., PlanRAG could in principle reach 98.7% on Locating given its 1.3% miss rate, vs 64.3% actual), separating retrieval/analysis completeness from reasoning quality. Standard IR metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are not used because retrieval is exact DBMS querying.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both. Outcome: decision accuracy (semantic match to ground-truth best decision). Process: rate of missed data analysis, SR/MR breakdown, failure-category analysis (CAN/MIS/DEEP/QUR/OTH), and number-of-re-plannings vs accuracy - all probing intermediate planning/retrieval quality, not only the final answer.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Not a primary focus; no token/latency/API-cost numbers are reported. The closest cost-related observation is the re-planning distribution (Table 7): Building re-plans more (38% of questions; 14.85% re-plan >4 times) than Locating (6%; 1.75% >4 times), and SingleRAG fails to retrieve any results in over 60% of Locating and 95% of Building questions (so extra iterative/planning steps are needed for correctness). The trade-off framing is accuracy/correctness vs prompt complexity (the complex PlanRAG prompt only works with a strong model like GPT-4 and breaks weaker models such as GPT-3.5/Llama-2/Phi-2).
context_budget_and_selection_count: Not explicitly budgeted as a fixed-k. The LM is given <Q, S, R> (question, full DB schema, business rules) plus the running plan and Observations; retrieved data are exactly what the generated SQL/Cypher queries return (variable size). The DB is too large to fit in context, motivating selective querying. Token-limit overflow is acknowledged only as an 'OTH' failure category. No reranked-then-truncated or fixed-k passage budget is defined.
survey_scope_and_axes: N/A (method + benchmark paper, not a survey).
benchmark_construction_and_size: DQA is reverse-engineered/transformed from two Paradox Interactive grand-strategy games (Europa Universalis IV for Locating, Victoria 3 for Building), chosen because they imitate real business decision situations. Size: 301 (Q, D) pairs (200 Locating, 101 Building); each question in both RDB and GDB -> 602 databases. Avg DB scale far exceeds prior Tabular QA/NLI (Locating RDB 2038.8 avg rows/table, Building 579.0, vs e.g. FinQA 6.26, HybridQA 15.7, TabFact 14.5). Construction: parse game savefiles into D per a fixed schema; generate Q from templates (Locating: 'Where should I locate my merchant? ... maximizing {COUNTRY_NODE}'s profit on home node {HOME_NODE}'; Building: 'Which building ID should we increase a level by 5 to maximally decrease the market price of {GOODS}?'); answers are deterministically annotated by purpose-built game SIMULATORS that apply business rules to every decision candidate and pick the best (verifiable ground-truth d_best). Quality control: Locating omits low-trading-power countries; Building filters questions with multiple answers. Released under MIT license (per Paradox EULA UGC clause); nation names anonymized to 3-letter codes for ethics. Best system (GPT-4 PlanRAG) reaches only 64.3% Locating / 45.0% Building, signaling the benchmark is hard.
builds_on: ReAct (Yao et al. 2023, Thought-Action-Observation backbone, extended with Plan/Re-plan instructions); iterative RAG (Trivedi et al. 2023 IRCoT; Jiang et al. 2023b FLARE; Shao et al. 2023) and single-turn RAG (Lewis et al. 2020; Guu et al. 2020 REALM; Izacard & Grave 2021; Izacard et al. 2023 Atlas); GPT-4 (OpenAI 2023) as the frozen base LM; LangChain and LlamaIndex as RAG/DB interfaces; Neo4j (Cypher/CQL, Francis et al. 2018) and MySQL as the DBMSs; structured-data reasoning benchmarks (Tabular QA / Table NLI) as conceptual predecessors.
contrasts_with: Existing single-turn and iterative RAG methods (IRCoT/FLARE-style, and the ReAct-based IterRAG baseline) that focus on knowledge-based QA and lack an explicit planning step - the paper argues they perform Steps (2) retrieval and (3) answering but not Step (1) planning, leading to disorganized querying and missed/improper data analysis. Also contrasts with prior Tabular QA / Table NLI benchmarks (HybridQA, TAT-QA, FinQA, WikiTableQA, TabFact, ToTTo-TNLI) which ignore business rules and use far smaller tables.
lineage: Group C (RAG + planning): a plan-then-retrieve / retrieve-then-plan agentic-RAG method. It sits in the lineage of iterative RAG (single-turn RAG -> IRCoT/FLARE iterative RAG -> ReAct agentic loop) and extends the ReAct family with explicit Plan and Re-plan reasoning for LLM-as-decision-maker over structured databases, simultaneously introducing the DQA decision-making benchmark.
cbr_cycle_coverage: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle over stored cases).
explicit_cbr_grounding: false. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is a plan-then-retrieval RAG technique.
tool_document_engineering: N/A (no tool/skill retrieval; data-analysis queries are generated against given DB schemas, not retrieved tools).
index_content_separation: Partial / implicit. The DB schema S and business rules R are given up-front to the LM (lightweight index) while the heavy data content of D is fetched on demand via generated SQL/Cypher queries (the database is too large to load into context), so there is a schema-then-content progressive-access pattern, though it is not framed as a designed index-content separation.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Live querying of an actual DBMS rather than a static document index: SQL executed against MySQL (RDB) and Cypher/CQL against Neo4j (GDB), mediated by LangChain/LlamaIndex. Not a tool-API/RapidAPI/MCP/function-calling tool store; no CRUD auto-sync of a tool index.
tool_dependency_awareness: N/A (no tools / inter-tool dependency modeling). The closest analogue is multi-hop graph traversal / multi-join data dependencies the plan must account for, but this is data dependency, not tool dependency.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (no case adaptation). The analogue is plan revision via the re-planning step (regenerate/correct the plan conditioned on intermediate query results), which is an LLM-prompted, execution-feedback-driven revision of the plan rather than adaptation of a retrieved case.
